title: Managing gilts through their first pregnancy
subtitle: Getting a first-parity sow to farrow in good condition with minimum problems.
excerpt: A gilt (a female pig that has not yet had her first litter) needs slightly different management from an established sow in the weeks leading up to her first farrowing. She is still growing herself while carrying a litter, has lower milk production potential than an experienced sow, and can become aggressive around farrowing due to unfamiliarity with the process. Getting her body condition, feeding, and environment right in the last six weeks of pregnancy significantly affects litter size at birth and her capacity to rear the piglets.

glossaryTerms.definition: A female pig that has not yet had her first litter. Once she has farrowed, she is called a sow. Gilts generally produce smaller first litters than established sows and have lower early milk production.

Increasing the feed intake of a gilt or sow in the two to three weeks before service to improve ovulation rate. Gilts flushed before mating typically produce larger litters, as more follicles reach maturity.

A visual and manual assessment of fat and muscle cover on a pig, scored on a 1 to 5 scale. Score 3 is ideal at farrowing: too lean (score 1 to 2) reduces milk supply; too fat (score 4 to 5) increases farrowing difficulty.

content.text: A
gilt

entering her first pregnancy is a growing animal herself, usually at 130 to 150 kg live weight at service. She needs enough feed to support her own growth and her litter simultaneously. The practical consequence is that gilts in first pregnancy need a slightly higher feed allowance than established sows of the same body size, particularly in the last four weeks.
Service and early pregnancy
The two weeks before service,
flush

the gilt: increase her feed intake by 0.5 to 1 kg per day above maintenance for 10 to 14 days pre-mating. This improves ovulation rate and sets up a larger potential litter. Drop back to a standard gestation ration immediately after confirmed mating.
Body condition through pregnancy
Assess
body condition score

at service, at 70 days, and at 100 days (two weeks before expected farrowing). The target at all three points is score 3. A gilt going into farrowing at score 2 (thin) will have reduced milk production and may struggle to rear a full litter. A gilt at score 4 or 5 (over-fat) has a higher risk of farrowing difficulty and is harder to manage in the farrowing pen.
Days 1 to 80: standard gestation ration at 2.2 to 2.5 kg per day (sow compound or a mix of barley and protein supplement with minerals). The gilt is growing alongside her embryos.
Days 80 to 100: increase to 2.5 to 3 kg per day. The foetuses grow 70% of their birth weight in the last 30 days; the gilt's nutrient requirements peak in this period.
Day 100 to farrowing: reduce to 2 kg per day and switch to a high-fibre ration if available. This reduces the risk of constipation at farrowing, which is a real issue in gilts.
Moving to the farrowing pen

Move the gilt to her farrowing pen at day 110 to 112 (three to five days before expected farrowing). This gives her time to familiarise herself with the space before the stress of farrowing, and allows her to begin nest-building behaviour. Gilts denied nest-building opportunities before farrowing show higher rates of savaging (attacking their own piglets) after birth.
At farrowing
Have someone present for the full farrowing of a gilt's first litter. Gilts have a higher rate of uterine inertia (stalled farrowing) and savaging than experienced sows.
If the gilt is showing aggression toward piglets, restrain her briefly while guiding each new piglet to a teat. Colostrum intake in the first hour is critical; a gilt that savages prevents this.
First-parity gilts often produce smaller litters (8 to 9 piglets) than their potential in subsequent litters (10 to 13). Do not cull a gilt on first-litter performance alone.

attrs.cue: Gilt attacks piglets after the first one or two are born
attrs.cause: Combination of pain, unfamiliarity, and oxytocin not yet fully established
attrs.fix: Restrain the gilt's head or use a temporary farrowing crate if one is available. Let the oxytocin of labour establish during the rest of the farrowing. Most gilts settle once they have farrowed the full litter and the piglets are nursing steadily.

attrs.cue: Gilt producing little milk on day two
attrs.cause: Mastitis or insufficient milk let-down rather than agalactia
attrs.fix: Check the udder: hot, hard, or uneven sections suggest mastitis and need immediate vet contact. If the udder is warm and even but not letting down, gentle massage and offering piglets frequently to stimulate can help. Thin gilt condition at farrowing is the most common underlying cause — address through the next pregnancy.
